# DNA barcoding: marker classifier model card

## Model

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Registered model | `dnabarcode-marker` |
| Version | 6 (alias `@candidate`) |
| Task | Predict which of 15 mitochondrial genes a sequence is from |
| Input | A DNA sequence (A, C, G, T; ambiguous bases allowed) |
| Output | One of 15 labels (or *reverse* for a sequence given as the other strand), with a confidence |
| Model | Logistic regression on 6-mer frequencies, rescaled to unit length, alpha 1e-06 |
| Calibration | Length-aware temperature, from v5 |
| Training data | MIDORI2 GB273 (15 genes), [doi:10.5281/zenodo.22685701](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22685701), CC-BY-4.0 |
| Built with | prokopton-ml 0.1.0 |

## Intended use

The marker classifier is the first check on every sequence: it predicts
which of the 15 mitochondrial genes the sequence comes from, and (by
comparing its confidence on both strands) which strand it was given as. If
the sequence is not COI, the site says which gene it looks like instead of
identifying it with the wrong model. Sequences of at least 100
bases are accepted.

It cannot yet reject sequences from other genomes or markers (such as plant
rbcL, fungal ITS or bacterial 16S, which are planned): it always picks the
most similar of the 15 genes, so it is used together with a similarity
check.

## Data

Records were split into training, validation and test sets; identical sequences always fall in the same set.

Training samples were capped at 20,000 records per class (validation: 2,000), spread across as many orders as possible.

| Sample | Records | Classes | Species per class |
|---|---|---|---|
| Training | 300,000 | 15 | 13,554 |
| Validation, known species | 30,000 | 15 | 1,811 |

## Training

2 candidate models were compared on the validation samples (never the test sets), and the best was chosen by the mean macro-F1 across them. Each training record also gave 1 random fragment of 75-600 bases, so the model learns short inputs too. Every candidate is recorded in MLflow (run `f31e98017c2f4275840a4e021016f5b5`).

| Validation set | Accuracy | Macro-F1 |
|---|---|---|
| Known species | 92.9% | 0.942 |
| Known species, fragments | 84.3% | 0.876 |

## Calibration

Confidence was corrected with a temperature that depends on length, T = exp(0.5600 - 0.1343 * ln(length)), fitted on the validation samples (whole sequences and new random fragments). It changes only confidence, never the prediction. *ECE* (expected calibration error) is the average gap between confidence and accuracy; 0 is perfect.

| Validation set | Accuracy | Mean confidence | ECE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Validation, known species | 92.9% | 85.9% → 91.3% | 0.070 → 0.016 |
| Validation, known species, fragments | 84.4% | 78.2% → 83.0% | 0.063 → 0.021 |

## Test results

Measured once, on test sets the model and its selection never saw. *Accuracy* counts every record equally; *macro-F1* gives every class equal weight, so rare groups count as much as common ones.

| Test set | Records | Accuracy | Top-5 | Macro-F1 | Confidence | ECE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Test set | 538,392 | 97.9% | 99.8% | 0.971 | 96.4% | 0.015 |

## Limitations

- **Short sequences** are much less accurate (at 100 bases, 72% accurate on the test set); below 100 bases they are declined.
- **Rare classes** have few reference records, so their scores vary more (see *Hardest classes*). Classes too rare to train on are never predicted.
- **The reference data reflects what has been sequenced**: GenBank holds far more records for some groups and regions than others, and some records are misidentified.
- **Only the 15 mitochondrial genes** are known; any other sequence is matched to the most similar of them, usually with low confidence.
- **Groups of organisms** are unevenly represented in some genes; see *By group of organisms*.
- **Confidence** is calibrated on validation data like the test data; on sequences unlike the reference data (contaminated, chimeric, or from a poorly sampled group) it may be too high.

## Development notes

These notes are written by hand and included in the generated card.

### Design

- **Labels** are the 15 mitochondrial genes in MIDORI2 (CO1, CO2, CO3, Cytb,
  A6 and A8 (ATP synthase 6 and 8), ND1-ND6 and ND4L, and the large and
  small ribosomal RNAs).
- **Avoiding a shortcut.** The genes are sequenced from very different
  organisms: CO1 records are mostly insects, while Cytb and the ribosomal
  RNAs are mostly vertebrates. A model could learn "fish-like means Cytb"
  rather than what each gene looks like. To prevent this, each gene's
  training records are spread across as many orders as possible, and the
  results are reported per group of organisms.
- **Strand.** Sequences may be given as either strand. Every training
  record's other strand (reverse complement) is added as a *reverse* class,
  so the model recognises a sequence given backwards. Both strands of a
  query are predicted, and the strand whose best gene is more confident is
  kept; the evaluation measures how often this picks the right strand.
- **Training on fragments and calibration** follow the router (see its
  card): one random fragment of 75-600 bases per record, and a
  length-aware temperature fitted on validation sequences and fragments.

### Version history

- **v1-v2** (one training run, then calibration): 98.6% accurate overall,
  but only 62% for fungi, and the other strand was more confident for 2%
  of animal and 34% of fungal records. An analysis
  (`analysis/04_marker_errors.py`) showed why. Most fungal errors were the
  two ribosomal RNAs mistaken for each other, and fungal protein-coding
  genes mistaken for ND2 or ND5: records were spread across orders, and
  animals have far more orders, so fungi were scarce in training. When the
  other strand won, it was mostly predicted as a *different* gene (a model
  error), not the record's own gene (which would mean a record stored
  backwards).
- **v3-v4:** records took turns between groups of organisms before
  orders, and the reverse class was added. The reverse class worked: the
  other strand was now more confident for only 0.5% of animal and 1.8% of
  fungal records. Balancing groups did not: fungi stayed at about 60%
  accurate, and animals fell from 99.5% to 98.3%. Naive Bayes was dropped
  from the search (0.870 against 0.915 for logistic regression in v1).
- **v5-v6:** records spread across orders again (as in v1), with the
  reverse class kept. 97.9% accurate overall (animals 98.9%, animal CO1
  99.8%), and the right strand is the more confident one for 99.6% of whole
  sequences (93% at 100 bases). Accuracy is slightly lower than v2's mostly
  because some records are predicted as *reverse*. On the site, the strand
  is chosen by the best gene and that gene is reported, so a *reverse* top
  answer never reaches users; the scores above are therefore cautious.

### Fungi

Fungal sequences remain the weak point (about 58-62% accurate in every
version), and more fungal training data did not help. A likely reason is biology rather
than sampling: fungal mitochondrial genes such as *cox1* (CO1), *cob*
(Cytb), *nad5* (ND5) and the large ribosomal RNA often contain many
introns, which can make up much of a record. A model that counts k-mers
across the whole record then sees mostly intron sequence, which these genes
share. This has not been tested here. For this site it matters little:
fungi are identified by ITS, not COI, and the marker classifier's main job
is to check animal COI.

### What it cannot do

It knows only these 15 genes. A sequence from another marker or genome is
still given one of them, so the site also checks how similar a sequence is
to the reference data, and says when a sequence is not recognised.
